summary: Short comments from Rand on the file transfer proposal in RFC 114. Rand sees a need for such a protocol and finds the proposal simple and extensible. It wants file transfer programs to have full access to local storage, including files they did not create.

plainLanguage.summary: A friend reads a plan for sharing files and says it looks good and easy. They only ask that the helper should be able to reach all files, not just the ones it made.

subtitle: Rand's short list of comments on the RFC 114 file transfer proposal: a good start, plus nine requests and questions.

tldr.problem: The file transfer proposal in RFC 114 needed feedback from sites that expected to implement it.
tldr.mechanism: Two Rand authors list nine comments: the protocol is needed and looks simple and extensible, file transfer programs should reach files they did not create, and several commands, status requests and error details should be added.
tldr.outcome: The comments are suggestions and a request for feedback on the MIT and Harvard experiments, not a specification.

today: RFC 141 updates RFC 114, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes it. It is a short set of 1971 review comments.

sections.title: General Support for the Proposal
sections.content:
The authors say a file transfer protocol is needed and that Bhushan's proposal in RFC 114 would meet a current need at their site as well as short-term needs they foresee. They find it straightforward to implement and extensible, as claimed.

The RFC's title says RFC 141, but the subject throughout is RFC 114.
sections.plainLanguage: The reviewers say the plan is useful and not hard to build, and that it can grow later.

sections.title: Requested Access and Commands
sections.content:
The authors want implementations where the file transfer program has general and complete access to local file storage. It should be able to retrieve a file that it did not create, for instance one a user made at site X independently of the file transfer program. This is not a requirement of RFC 114, but they would like to see it where possible.

Because a subset of transaction types is explicitly permitted, they suggest adding commands to insert, delete and replace records within a file, which they have used with a non-standard file subsystem under IBM OS/360. They also want a way to get the names of files under their access control, in addition to retrieve and lookup.
sections.plainLanguage: They ask that the helper be able to open any file on the computer, and that it can also add, remove or swap lines inside a file.

sections.title: Status, Execute and Errors
sections.content:
The authors note that status requests and responses are absent. Since an execute request exists, they would like to ask about the status of the process it creates, especially if execution is implemented like remote job entry and scheduling may take a long time.

On execute, the using host sends parameters after the rr response. For their 360, the authors prefer the attach macro, which starts an independent task, but that needs parameters at start. So they want either the parameters included in the execute command or no start until parameters arrive. On abnormal termination, the reply should include part or all of the offending request and an identifying code so the error is recognized precisely.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask the helper to run a job, you should be able to ask how it is going. If something goes wrong, the helper should say exactly what failed.

sections.title: Asking About Experiments
sections.content: The last comment asks for the outcome of the MIT and Harvard experiments with the RFC 114 protocol, including any pitfalls found. The RFC reports no results itself.
sections.plainLanguage: They also ask the first testers to tell everyone what went wrong, so others can learn from it.

references.text: Bhushan, A., A File Transfer Protocol, RFC 114.
